name: ui/markdown-renderer
title: MarkdownRenderer
summary: Markdown, safe by construction: parsed into a typed tree and drawn as elements, never through an HTML string. Raw HTML in the source is text; links pass a scheme allow-list. One contract for the Astro, React and Mzizi Roots builds.

props.name: content
props.description: The Markdown to show (or, with `from`, rich-text HTML). Untrusted text is fine: it is never parsed as HTML.

props.name: links
props.description: safe keeps http, https, mailto, tel and relative addresses; https keeps https only. A refused link keeps its words and loses its address.

props.name: from
props.description: What content is. html reads an editor's rich text into Markdown first (a reader of its own that builds plain data, never a DOM, so nothing in it runs; the same on a server, in a browser and in Rust); auto does so when the text holds an editor's tags. Text in rich text stays text: Markdown typed into an editor is not read as Markdown.

props.name: headingBase
props.description: The heading level a `#` heading renders at (1 to 6); deeper levels follow and stop at h6. Lets the text sit under a page's own headings.

behaviour: The Markdown is parsed into a typed tree (blocks and inlines) and the tree is rendered as elements. No build has an HTML string sink: no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, no set:html, no dangerous_inner_html.

Blocks: paragraphs (every line break is a hard break; a backslash at the end of a line is dropped only when another line follows, so on the last line it is text), ATX headings, bulleted and numbered lists nested by indentation (a numbered list keeps its first number; as in CommonMark, a list interrupts a paragraph, or the text of the item before it, only when its first item has text and, if numbered, is numbered 1, so a line such as "1984. was a year" stays in its paragraph; an item indented between two levels joins the deeper list), blockquotes, fenced code (``` or ~~~, the info word as data-language), horizontal rules and GFM tables with column alignment.
Inlines: code spans, links, bold (** or __), italic (* or _), bold italic (***), backslash escapes. A marker with no partner, and an underscore inside a word, stay text.
Raw HTML in the source is text:

Links: tabs and newlines anywhere, and controls and spaces at either end, are removed first (browsers ignore them), then an address with whitespace still inside is refused, the scheme is checked against an allow-list, and a web address (http, https or //host) needs a host the URL parser accepts, no credentials (https://bank.example@evil.example is refused) and no port but a number up to 65535 (https://example.com:abc/ and :99999 are refused). A mailto address whose domain the URL parser rejects is refused too. A refused link renders its words with no element around them. http and https links open in a new tab with rel="noopener noreferrer".

A kept link shows its address on hover: its title is the address normalised for reading, with the scheme and host lower-cased and the host in ASCII as the WHATWG URL parser serialises it (an internationalised host as punycode, so https://аpple.com shows as https://xn--pple-43d.com), and the rest as written. A mailto address shows each domain the same way (mailto:help@аpple.com shows as mailto:help@xn--pple-43d.com). Its href stays as written. Every build gives the same title (TypeScript: the URL parser's hostname; Rust: the url crate's host parser, through idna). Where TypeScript has no URL global, it keeps only the hosts it can normalise exactly as the parser does (plain ASCII names and dotted-decimal IPv4 addresses) and refuses the rest, so a kept link's title does not depend on the runtime.

A link's address ends at the first space or ASCII control character, as in CommonMark (a title after it is dropped). Other whitespace, such as a no-break space, is part of the address, so the link is refused rather than sent to the part before it. Backslash escapes of ASCII punctuation in it are undone, as in CommonMark: [a](x.org/\(y\)) goes to x.org/(y).
A link inside a link's words renders as its words.
Nesting is bounded: lists and blockquotes 8 deep, inline marks 16 deep; deeper markers read as text.
Hostile text stays linear: each inline parse has a scanning budget (100000 steps plus 32 per character); when it runs out, markers still looking for a partner read as text.

Rich text (from=html or auto): block elements and
end lines, source newlines are spaces, list items are one line each with their nested lists kept (to 8 deep; a list placed directly in a list, as Google Docs and Word paste one, nests under the item before it) and
    kept, a
    in 
     is a line break (only a source newline right after 
     is dropped), and text after a nested list follows it in order, bold, italic, code and links keep their meaning, script-like elements are dropped with their content up to the end tag a browser ends them at: a text element (script, style, textarea, …) at its own end tag (, so  does not end a script; inside  or --!>), a doctype and other bogus comments (, , ) are read as the HTML tokenizer reads them, so none shows as text. Every other tag is a plain container.

gaps: Not CommonMark-complete: no setext headings, indented code blocks, reference links, autolinks, footnotes, task lists or strikethrough.

Rich text: tables and images in an editor's HTML are read as text (cells flattened to lines), not rebuilt, and a list item's own paragraphs are joined into one line. A list placed directly in a list before any item gets an item of its own with no line, so it shows an empty marker (and in a numbered list takes a number) where a browser shows none.

List nesting is by indentation relative to the list an item is in (two or more spaces deeper nests), not by the previous item's content column as in CommonMark, so after a wide marker such as `10.` or a staircase of uneven indents an item can nest one level differently.

Rich text: the reader follows the HTML tokenizer and the tree-building rules that decide where a dropped element ends, checked against a spec-compliant parser, but it is not a full HTML tree builder. Where a document relies on rarer rules, a dropped element can end at a different end tag than in a browser: usually later, so more is dropped (for example after a tag such as
